To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the majority of the 2,500 children in the cohort had a normal weight-for-age at birth, 2) the majority of children who were underweight at birth had a normal weight at 24 months, and 3) the majority of underweight children who had a low weight at 24 month were born underweight.
The results of the present research indicate that the use of the internet for health info and health-associated social networking is widespread among young adults.
the use of the WHO growth standards for the first 24 months of life is associated with a higher prevalence of stunting and underweight, and a higher prevalence of high increments of overweight along.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the two most common measures of growth in infancy, weight-for-age and length-for-age.
the relationship between growth and body fatness.
the relationship between growth and overweight during the first 2 years of life.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a child who is born with low birth weight and who is breastfed for a long time, is likely to be small and thin at age two years.
the prevalence of overweight is increasing in all regions of the world and is now a global public health problem of major importance.

the most important factor in the development of overweight in the early stages of life is the interaction between genetics and environment, and that the environment in which children grow up plays a decisive role in the development of childhood overweight.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the prevalence of overweight in the first 24 weeks of life is higher in children from low- and middle-income countries than in children from high-income countries, and that overweight during this period is associated with low growth.
the most important factor in the development of the obesity epidemic is a change in the way we live.
a child's growth in the initial 24 months is a strong indicator of his/her risk of being overweight in adulthood.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are a number of factors that contribute to the development of overweight and obesity, and that there is a need to address the underlying causes of these conditions.
the first year of life is a critical window of opportunity for preventing childhood obesity.
we need to do more to help families who are at risk for obesity.
